chunks: "The big difference is how you control them.
A BJT is a bipolar, junction device: you forward-bias the base-emitter junction, and to keep it on you have to keep supplying base current, roughly the collector current divided by beta.
A MOSFET is a field-effect device with an insulated gate: you apply a voltage, the field creates a channel, and once the gate capacitance is charged it takes essentially zero current to stay on.
That leads to the practical differences.
When fully on, a BJT has a roughly fixed V CE(sat) of a couple hundred millivolts or more, while a MOSFET acts like a resistor, R DS(on) , which can be milliohms.
MOSFETs switch faster because they're majority-carrier devices, with no stored charge to pull out of a saturated base.
And MOSFETs parallel more easily because R DS(on) rises with temperature, whereas a BJT tends toward thermal runaway.

BJTs still win in some places: they have higher transconductance per milliamp, I C over V T , about 39 mS per mA, and lower 1 over f noise, so they're good for precision analog, and they turn on at a predictable 0.
6–0. 7 volts. One trap: the regions are named confusingly. A BJT in saturation is fully on, like a switch, but a MOSFET in saturation is the constant-current amplifier region.
The MOSFET's switch region is triode."
